atoms.b: Hey! Where does the name “woodwind” actually come from?
Good question! Let’s take a look at the word. It is a compound noun made up of ((++two three)) parts: <m-blue>wood</m-blue> and <m-yellow>wind </m-yellow>.
“Wind” is pretty clear! Sound is made when you blow ((++air sand)) — or “wind” — into the instrument.
Sure, but why “wood”? The recorder, oboe, clarinet and bassoon are made of wood, but the silver flute and the brass ((++saxophone telephone)) are made of metal...
There are two reasons for this. Firstly, almost all of these instruments were made of ((++wood wax)) in the past.
Yes, but not the saxophone! That has always been made of metal.
That’s true, but the saxophone gives us the second reason: it’s not made entirely of metal! Its ((++mouthpiece body)) is made of wood.
The “mouthpiece”... is that the part that you play with your ((++mouth thumb)) when you blow into it?
Yes, exactly! The name “woodwind” primarily describes the special way in which the ((++sounds pounds)) are made.
